Notes

屌不屌

屌 is profane, but as an adjective it can praise someone as formidable or impressive. “Badass or what?” keeps the boast and its rough register. Later, 草 functions as a sound-alike spelling of the swear 操, not as literal grass.

  • Genius community transcript
鲜花掌声

Flowers and applause initially look like rewards for performing, but they already cover a body. The song later supplies a tombstone, coffin, and burial clothes. That sequence lets the same image move from public adoration toward a funeral, making success and disposal disturbingly close.

  • Lyric text
哟哟哟切克闹

The pairing of “check it out” with 来一套 echoes the jianbing snack rhyme documented in this Nankai Youth League food article. Here the familiar order for a set is filled with a coffin and burial clothes. This identifies the textual resemblance, not a confirmed statement of the artist’s intent.

  • Nankai Youth League — jianbing rhyme in use (2017)
一套

Earlier 戴套 means wearing a condom; here 一套 means a complete set. The character 套 links the sexualized exchange for money and fame to the sale of a coffin with burial clothes.

  • Genius community transcript
跳大神

跳大神 names spirit-invoking ritual performance involving dancing and incantation, traditionally associated with seeking protection or driving away misfortune. The lyric adds an obscene performance instruction to it; “Kai” later uses the same expression inside its grotesque caveman image. That sacred-to-derisive shift matters more here than the literal act of dancing.

  • Ministry of Education dictionary: 跳大神
  • Kai lyric text
  • Lyric text
高考完后的学校

The gaokao is China’s national college entrance exam. A documented post-exam celebration involves throwing study materials into the air; this gives a concrete visual context for the preceding stacks of money flying. The photograph is contextual evidence, not the identified event behind the lyric.

  • China Daily — students tossing study materials after the gaokao (2013)
圈套

套 has already appeared in 戴套, wearing a condom, and 一套, a complete set of funeral goods. 圈套 adds the sense of a trap or setup. This third use turns the repeated character into a chain connecting sex, sales, and manipulation.

  • Lyric text
世界大草帽

The supplied Genius text reads “world / big straw hat.” The phrase is awkward in context and may need correction after listening. The English keeps the literal image and marks the uncertainty rather than replacing it with a more familiar saying.

  • Genius community transcript
狗屁

狗屁 literally means dog fart, but its ordinary insulting force is “nonsense” or “bullshit.” The Chinese animal-and-smell image becomes an English excrement idiom rather than a literal canine event. Repeating it after the grand claims of fame and praise collapses those claims into something worthless.

  • Lyric text
